topicCandidates: The distinct roles of a visa, Certificate of Eligibility, landing permission, status of residence, period of stay, and residence card.
The ordinary long-term entry sequence from route and sponsor selection through COE, consular visa application, landing examination, and post-arrival residence registration.
COE scope, ordinary three-month validity, electronic or printed presentation, and the fact that a COE does not guarantee visa issuance or landing permission.
Work-status selection based on actual principal duties, contract and organization facts, qualifications or licensing, remuneration, and adjacent-status exclusions rather than job title alone.
The boundary between visa-exempt or Temporary Visitor entry and permission to perform income-earning activity.
Extension of period of stay versus change of status of residence, their application windows, discretionary review, and the special pending-application period.
Covered resident notifications after a contract, employer, school, or other affiliated-organization change, kept separate from employer-side reporting duties.
The optional Certificate of Authorized Employment as evidence about permitted work activity, without treating it as a status change or approval of unrelated work.
Status-maintenance risks when the authorized principal activity stops, including category-specific inactivity periods and individualized justifiable-reason review.
Special re-entry permission for eligible short trips, its one-year ceiling, the earlier period-of-stay expiry, required departure declaration, and exclusions.
Ordinary single or multiple re-entry permission for longer absences, limited by both its grant and the existing period of stay.
Travel while an extension or change application is pending, including the shortened return-and-decision deadline created by the special pending-application period.
Lost passports or residence cards abroad, proof of the re-entry deadline for carrier checks, and post-return residence-card replacement.

Temporary departure versus permanent departure, including residence-card return when a planned return no longer occurs and handoffs to municipal, tax, pension, insurance, housing, and account closure guidance.
userSituations: A first-time long-term entrant who has received a COE and needs to understand what remains undecided before boarding and at the airport.
A visa-exempt traveler considering paid work or a stay longer than the short-stay allowance.
A professional comparing two work statuses whose job title is ambiguous but whose actual duties, qualifications, contract, and institution are known.
A resident approaching expiry who is unsure whether to extend the current status or change to a different residence purpose.
A worker who has resigned, joined a new employer, or changed contracts and needs to separate notification duties from permission to perform the new work.
A resident who has stopped the principal authorized activity while job searching, ill, studying elsewhere, or waiting for a new contract.
A student or worker taking a short trip abroad and expecting to return under the existing status of residence.
A resident planning to remain abroad for more than one year but return before the current period of stay expires.
A resident whose period of stay will expire while abroad or who needs to travel while an extension or change application is pending.
A traveler who loses a passport or residence card abroad and may need proof of Japanese residence status to board the return flight.
A person who left under re-entry arrangements but later decides not to return and must close out the residence record properly.
edgeCasesAndExceptions: A COE normally expires three months after issuance; an old pandemic-era validity extension must not be presented as current general policy.
A COE certifies a landing-condition category but does not guarantee a visa, and a visa remains only one condition for landing rather than permission to enter by itself.
A visa-exemption allowance generally assumes a short stay without income-earning activity; nationality-specific consular rules and multiple-entry visas remain separate questions.
A change application allows a person to request a different status without leaving Japan, but filing alone must not be described as authorization to begin activity outside the current status.
Extension applications are generally accepted up to three months before expiry for periods of six months or more; shorter periods use a different opening rule.
When a timely extension or change application remains undecided at expiry, the special period ends at the decision or two months after the old expiry date, whichever comes first.

Travel during a pending application is possible with valid re-entry arrangements, but the resident must remain reachable and return and receive the decision before the applicable special-period deadline.
A resident notification within 14 days applies only to covered statuses and events; the former or new organization may have a separate reporting duty with different forms and deadlines.
Submitting an organization-change notification does not establish that duties at the new organization fit the current status.

Status revocation is not automatic on day 91 without activity; the legal category, duration, alternative activity, and justifiable reason require individualized assessment, and Highly Skilled Professional (ii) uses a different period.
Special re-entry permission excludes Temporary Visitor and people granted a period of stay of three months or less, as well as specifically listed enforcement or public-interest cases.
Special re-entry expires at the earlier of one year after departure and the current period-of-stay expiry and cannot be extended abroad.

Ordinary re-entry permission can be single-use or multiple-use and may be granted for up to five years, but never beyond the current period of stay; special permanent residents follow different periods.

A period-of-stay extension cannot be filed at a Japanese embassy abroad. Limited consular extension of an ordinary re-entry permit is a separate procedure and cannot extend the underlying period of stay.

A residence card lost abroad does not necessarily prevent re-entry, but airlines may request proof; after return, the holder generally must apply for replacement within 14 days of re-entry or learning of the loss, as applicable.

A person who leaves temporarily and later abandons the return may acquire a residence-card return obligation; this differs from surrendering the card as a permanent departure at the port of departure.

Permanent Resident status has no period-of-stay expiry but the residence card itself expires and re-entry permission remains relevant; Special Permanent Resident rules must not be generalized to other residents.
jurisdictionVariables: Immigration Services Agency rules for landing, residence status, residence applications, notifications, residence cards, and re-entry.
Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the responsible embassy or consulate for visa issuance, nationality-specific documentation, and overseas procedures.
Airline or carrier document checks, which may require practical proof beyond the legal elements of re-entry.
Municipal residence registration and moving-out procedures after immigration decisions.
Employer reporting to the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, separate from the resident's Immigration Services Agency notification.
Professional licensing, employment, tax, pension, health-insurance, and municipal obligations that are affected by a move or job change but are not decided by immigration permission.
Individual regional immigration examination and discretion; local procedural practice must not be represented as a different national eligibility rule.

contentImpacts.reason: Turn the overview into the canonical decision chain separating visa, COE, landing permission, status, period of stay, and residence card.
Ground route selection in actual duties, organization, contract, qualifications or licensing, remuneration, and adjacent-status exclusions, then connect it to the structured status pilot.
Add a precise pre-departure decision and document sequence, COE validity checks, changed-circumstance warnings, and arrival handoffs without duplicating municipal guidance.
Explain extension versus change, filing windows, special-period deadlines, pending-application travel, discretionary review, and safe next actions.
Separate resident and employer notifications from work authorization, add status/event applicability, and explain when a Certificate of Authorized Employment may help.
Make permanent departure explicit, link temporary travelers to dedicated re-entry guidance, and cover a later decision not to return.
Provide one reusable guide for ordinary and special re-entry, competing deadlines, pending applications, exclusions, document loss, and return planning across journeys.
Answer the ordinary-language question about leaving Japan temporarily without losing the current residence route and link to the dedicated guide.
Add pending-application timing and travel language without turning the FAQ into an individualized eligibility answer.
Clarify resident-versus-employer duties and that notification alone does not authorize new duties.
Introduce ordinary re-entry permission with pronunciation, plain-language meaning, and the separate permission and status-expiry clocks.
Introduce special re-entry permission and distinguish it from ordinary re-entry permission.
Explain the special pending-application period and its deadline without describing it as an automatic two-month extension.
Add temporary travel and re-entry as a focused optional branch instead of placing permanent-departure guidance in the travel path.

scopeBoundaries: Iteration 3B should revise the six assigned foundation articles, create the dedicated re-entry guide, add the directly required glossary and FAQ records, and connect relevant journeys; it should not rewrite every route-specific article.

The guides may explain official categories, timing, evidence, and decision points but must not decide an individual's eligibility, predict approval, or replace Immigration Services Agency or consular advice.
The re-entry guide should be shared across student, work, family, business, and other eligible residence journeys rather than copied into each route article.

Temporary Visitor, multiple-entry visa, refugee-applicant, enforcement, Special Permanent Resident, and passportless-travel cases require explicit boundaries and must not inherit the ordinary mid-to-long-term resident summary.

Arrival guidance should stop at the handoff to residence-card and municipal registration guides; municipal, My Number, insurance, pension, banking, housing, and phone procedures remain separate reusable content.
Permanent-departure guidance may identify tax, pension, insurance, housing, banking, utilities, and municipal handoffs but detailed legal rules remain in their later research workstreams.
Employer reporting, professional licensing, employment law, and tax consequences must be labeled as separate authority domains even when linked from a job-change guide.
No researched assertion or revised article becomes editorially approved without explicit human review; implementation should retain the existing needs-review state.

scopeApproval.note: Approved all five recommendations: shared optional re-entry placement, duplicated source-backed pending-travel warning, compact resident-versus-employer distinction, Certificate of Authorized Employment retained within the contract-change guide, and one permanent-departure guide pending later tax and municipal research.
